head coach.) [Dynasties and Counterpunches](../11-history/11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd)
tells the story of that rule and the passing boom that followed.

**Offenses learned to live in the seam.** A Tampa 2 Mike carrying a tight end up the middle was a
fair fight in 1999. Against a 6-foot-6 tight end who ran like a receiver, or a slot receiver
lined up as the inside man in a trips formation, it wasn't. Offenses also learned to attack the
hole the Mike vacates, with digs and curls that sit down 12 to 15 yards deep in front of him, and
to flood the sideline holes the squat corners leave. Peyton Manning, who practised against Dungy's
Tampa 2 every day in Indianapolis, became one of the best at taking it apart (that, too, is in
[Dynasties and Counterpunches](../11-history/11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd)).

**The Mikes were rare.** A middle linebacker who can stop the run between the tackles and also
run 20 yards with a receiver is one of the rarest athletes in the sport. Teams that copied the
scheme without one found out quickly what Cover 2 without a deep middle defender looks like.

**Light boxes met better run games.** A two-deep, four-rush defense lives with six or seven
defenders near the line. That was survivable when offenses lined up in two-back formations and ran
into the teeth of it; it was less survivable against spread formations that thinned the box further
and against run games designed to exploit it.

**Then the league went one-high, and then two-high again, but differently.** Through the early
2010s the fashionable answer to everything was Pete Carroll's Seattle Cover 3, a single-high
defense with press corners and an eighth defender near the line
([The Cover 3 Family](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)). (Gus Bradley, Seattle's defensive coordinator from 2009 to 2012,
had coached linebackers under Kiffin in Tampa.) When two-high defense came back after 2018, it
came back as **quarters and match coverage**: two safeties who read the receivers in front of them
and fit the run, not two safeties guarding halves while the Mike runs the middle
([Quarters and the Two-High Match Family](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd)).

### What survived

A great deal, just not under its old name.

- **Cover 2 itself.** It never left. Next Gen Stats counted 13.9 percent of 2025 dropbacks as Cover
  2 (the source is in the note on 2-Man's situations), and the FTN charting in nflverse labels even
  more; it remains a standard call on long yardage, at the end of halves, and as a change-up for
  defenses whose base is something else.
- **The Mike who carries the seam.** "The middle defender carries #3 vertical" (if the third
  receiver from the sideline runs straight up the field, the middle linebacker runs with him) is now
  a rule in Cover 3 match and quarters, the descendants of spot-drop zone. Any time you see a linebacker turn
  and run with a tight end up the middle of the field in a modern zone, that's the Tampa 2 Mike's
  job inside a newer coverage ([Cover 3 match](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-3-match)).
- **Two-high pictures that become three-deep.** The Tampa 2's real trick was showing two deep
  safeties and playing with three deep defenders after the snap. Modern defenses do the same thing
  by rotating a safety instead of running the Mike, and that is the whole subject of
  [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).
- **Cover 2 as half a coverage.** Cover 6 plays quarters to one side and Cover 2 to the other,
  squat corner and all; split-field defenses use the Cover 2 half to the short side of the field
  or against a formation's lone receiver ([Quarters and the Two-High Match Family](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd)).
- **2-Man on third down,** as the chart above shows.
- **The people.** The Tampa staffs of 1996–2008 seeded a generation of NFL coaches. Lovie Smith and
  Rod Marinelli took the system to Chicago and Detroit; Mike Tomlin, Tampa Bay's defensive backs
  coach from 2001 to 2005, and Raheem Morris, who worked his way up the same secondary, became head
  coaches.[^tree] The approach (simple calls, fast players, eyes on the quarterback, rally to the ball)
  outlived the coverage, and a branch of the tree, Matt Eberflus, ran some of the most Cover 2-heavy
  defenses of the charting era in Indianapolis and Chicago.[^eberflus]

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the squat-corner spotter"}
On every passing down for one quarter, look at the cornerbacks first.

- **Before the snap.** Corners 5 to 7 yards off, a step *outside* the wide receiver, flat-footed,
  shoulders turned in toward the ball? Two safeties deep (12 to 14 yards) and wide (outside the
  hashes)? Think **Cover 2**. Corners pressed on the receiver's *inside* shoulder on third-and-long?
  Lean **2-Man**, but confirm it after the snap. Corners 7 or 8 off with two safeties deep? It may be
  quarters ([Quarters and the Two-High Match Family](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd)), or a Cover 2 that
  squats only at the snap ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).
- **At the snap.** Does the corner punch the receiver and then *stop*, hips square, eyes on the
  quarterback, while the receiver runs past? Cover 2. Does he turn his hips and run with him, eyes on
  the receiver? 2-Man (or a disguise into something else).
- **One second later.** Find the Mike. Did he stop at 10 yards, eyes on the quarterback? Cover 2.
  Is he still running straight down the middle at 15? **Tampa 2.**
- **When the ball is thrown.** Where did it go? A sideline throw between the corner and the safety,
  or a seam between the safeties, is the offense attacking exactly the holes this chapter mapped.
  A completed 6-yard out on third-and-12, followed by an immediate tackle, is the coverage winning.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: one squat corner"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-squat
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10 at midfield, ball in the middle of the field. Two safeties deep. The left corner is 5 yards off X, a step outside him; the right corner is 8 yards off Z, nearly head-up. The cornerbacks and safeties are ringed. Use the depth numbers on the left and the hash marks along the bottom."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = [p.moved(d=8.0, w=15.4) if p.key == "RCB" else p
       for p in c2_shell(off, corner_d=5.0, safety_d=13.0, safety_w=10.0)]
pr1 = Play(off, dfn, los=60, to_go=10)
pr1.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "FS", "SS")
fld = pr1.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 17.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr1, widths=True)
plt.show()
```

**The two corners disagree. Which coverages fit this picture, which side would you attack with
smash or a hole shot, and what would you check in the first second after the snap?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Several coverages fit; the left side means the same thing in all of them.** A two-high shell
with one squat corner could be plain Cover 2 (the right corner will squat at the snap), Cover 6
(Cover 2 on the left, quarters on the right; see
[Quarters and the Two-High Match Family](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd)), or Cover 3 with a cloud
rotation to the left, where the left safety runs to the deep outside third and the other safety
spins to the middle ([The Cover 3 Family](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)).

**Attack the left.** In every one of those, the left corner is a flat defender with a safety coming
from inside and deep to cover the sideline behind him. Smash (hitch by X, corner route by H) or a go
route by X with H up the seam attacks exactly that grass. Smash is a high-low on the squat corner
whatever the coverage behind him; that's why it's a favourite call against a squat corner you can see.

**Then check, in the first second:** does one safety race to the middle of the field? Then it's
cloud Cover 3, the deep middle is closed, and the hole shot is against a safety running to his third.
Do both safeties stay on their sides? Then it's Cover 2 or Cover 6, and the right corner tells you
which: squatting at the snap means Cover 2, backpedalling to a deep quarter means Cover 6.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the tight end up the middle"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-trips
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-7. Trips to the offense's right: Z (#1), H (#2) and the tight end Y (#3), in-line. The defense shows a two-high shell with squat corners. On this play Y will run straight up the middle of the field. The Mike (M) and Y are ringed."
off = offense("gun_trips")
dfn = c2_shell(off, corner_d=5.5)
mv = {"NB": (5.0, 9.5), "MIKE": (4.5, 2.0), "WILL": (5.0, -4.0)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1]) if p.key in mv else p for p in dfn]
pr2 = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7)
pr2.route("Y", r.path((2.0, 0.6), (12.0, -3.5), (22.0, -4.0)))
pr2.highlight("MIKE", "Y")
fld = pr2.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 24))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr2, widths=True)
plt.show()
```

**(a) If this is plain Cover 2 played by the book, who has Y? (b) What would you watch in the first
second to know whether it's Tampa 2? (c) The defense has seen this formation all game. What might it
have changed, and where would you look for it before the snap?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**(a) By the book, almost nobody.** The Mike drops to the hole at 10 to 12 yards and watches Y run
past him. The trips-side safety has three receivers in his half, and the outside two are running
routes he can't ignore; the far safety is guarding the left half and X. Y ends up in the deep
middle, between the two safeties: thin spot ③. This is the classic way to attack Cover 2 from trips.

**(b) The Mike.** At one second, is he still running, opening toward the trips side and getting
on top of Y? That is Tampa 2: the Mike carries #3 up the pipe, which is exactly the throw it was
built to take away. Then the question becomes *who* is running up the middle. A big, slow tight end
against a fast linebacker is a fair fight; a fast tight end or a slot receiver against a linebacker
15 yards downfield is not. And the dig by H, sitting down at 12 to 14 yards where the Mike used to
be, is open underneath him.

**(c) Look at the backside safety, the one on X's side.** He has only X in his half, and his corner
is already sitting short on X's side, so the most common adjustment is to give him #3: he cheats a couple of
yards toward the middle before the snap, or he drifts there at the snap, and Y's seam runs into him.
Other defenses hand #3 to the Mike every snap, or check out of Cover 2 entirely against trips
([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)). A
backside safety narrower than his partner is your pre-snap hint.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-8, two-high, corners outside"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2man
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-8. Two safeties 13 yards deep. Both corners are 5 yards off, a step outside their receivers; the Will (W) is 5 yards off over the slot receiver H and the nickel ($) over the tight end Y. The ringed defenders are the five possible man defenders. The quarterback is a good runner."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
pr3 = Play(off, c2_shell(off, corner_d=5.0, safety_d=13.0), los=45, to_go=8)
pr3.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "NB", "WILL", "MIKE")
fld = pr3.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 17.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr3, widths=True)
plt.show()
```

**Cover 2 or 2-Man? Which is more likely, what single thing would you watch in the first second,
and how would you design the pass so the quarterback has an answer either way?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**You can't be sure, and that is the point of the alignment.** Third-and-8 is where 2-Man peaks, but
even there Cover 2 is called about twice as often: on third or fourth and 7 to 10, the charting
behind the down-and-distance chart has Cover 2 on roughly 12 to 17 percent of dropbacks and 2-Man on
6 to 10. And the corners are
showing Cover 2's alignment, off and outside, not the press-inside look of a 2-Man lean. So the
base rate says Cover 2, with 2-Man very much alive.

**Watch the corners' hips and eyes.** If a corner opens his hips and runs with his receiver, eyes on
him, it's 2-Man. If he stays square, eyes on the quarterback, and lets the receiver go, it's Cover 2.

**Design for both.** Offenses facing this picture often put a zone-beater on one side and a
man-beater on the other and let the quarterback pick after the snap: smash to one side (it beats
the squat corner in zone), and a rub or an out-breaking route to the other (it beats a man defender
playing inside leverage). And if it is 2-Man and nobody is open, the quarterback's legs are the
answer: five defenders have their backs to him, unless the one on the running back has been told to
rush or spy. Throwing deep is the one thing not to do: two safeties are waiting there either way.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Cover 2 is two deep and five under.** The safeties each guard a deep half; the corners guard
  the flats; three linebackers (or two and a nickel) guard the hook-curl zones and the hole. It
  takes away the short throws and everything over the top, and it costs a defender in the box.
- **The hard (squat) corner is the tell.** Five to seven yards off, outside leverage, eyes inside;
  at the snap he jams, sinks and sits in the flat. When you see two of them with two deep safeties,
  think Cover 2, then confirm it after the snap: a corner whose hips turn to run with the receiver
  is playing 2-Man.
- **Cover 2's thin spots are known by heart:** the hole shot along the sideline, the smash corner
  over the squat corner (the same grass, reached from inside), the deep middle between the safeties,
  and the intermediate sideline hole. Deep passes go to the middle against Cover 2 about one time in
  three, as often as or more often than against any other coverage in the charting data.
- **Tampa 2 sends the Mike down the middle:** five underneath at the snap, then four under and three
  deep. It closes the deep middle, needs a rare linebacker, opens the intermediate middle (dagger
  and levels live there), and is Cover 2's best answer to trips. It was the
  identity of Dungy and Kiffin's Buccaneers, Dungy's Colts and Lovie Smith's Bears.
- **2-Man keeps the two deep safeties and plays man underneath,** in trail technique with inside
  leverage. It's a long-yardage and end-of-half call, vulnerable to scrambles, rubs and out-breaking
  routes.
- **Classic Tampa 2 faded** (contact rules, seam-stretching offenses, rare Mikes, light boxes, the
  move to Cover 3 and then to quarters), **but its pieces survive:** Cover 2 as a call, the
  seam-carrying middle defender, two-high pictures that become three-deep, and a large coaching tree.

[^when]: This book's calculation from the same nflverse data as the deep-pass figure (regular-season dropbacks 2018–2025 with a charted coverage). 2-Man share by situation, NGS seasons / FTN seasons: first down 1.1% / 5.2%; third or fourth and 7–10 yards 6.4% / 9.7%; third or fourth and 11+ 5.1% / 8.1%; in the last two minutes of either half 4.4% / 9.2%, against 1.7% / 5.8% at other times. Cover 2: third or fourth and 1–2 yards 8.0% / 13.8%, third or fourth and 7–10 yards 11.9% / 17.4%, first down 13.6% / 20.9%. Season shares of Cover 2 in the nflverse labels: 12.7–14.1% in 2018–2022 (NGS), 16.3%, 21.1% and 23.0% in 2023–2025 (FTN).

[^ngs]: NFL Next Gen Stats via NFL.com, "The coverage that turned the Seahawks into Super Bowl winners and is taking the NFL by storm": https://www.nfl.com/news/the-coverage-that-turned-the-seahawks-into-super-bowl-winners-and-is-taking-the-nfl-by-storm (2025 coverage shares on dropbacks: Cover 4 17.2%, Cover 2 13.9%, Cover 6 9.2%). Next Gen Stats' own 2025 figure is lower than the FTN labels in nflverse (23.0%); the two charters classify coverages differently.
